# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Grain Stocks 

ISSN: 1949-0925

Released January 12, 2026, by the National Agricultural Statistics Service 
(NASS), Agricultural Statistics Board, United States Department of 
Agriculture (USDA).

Corn Stocks Up 10 Percent from December 2024
Soybean Stocks Up 6 Percent
All Wheat Stocks Up 7 Percent

Corn stored in all positions on December 1, 2025 totaled 13.3 billion 
bushels, up 10 percent from December 1, 2024. Of the total stocks, 
8.70 billion bushels are stored on farms, up 14 percent from a year earlier. 
Off-farm stocks, at 4.58 billion bushels, are up 4 percent from a year ago. 
The September - November 2025 indicated disappearance is 5.29 billion 
bushels, compared with 4.58 billion bushels during the same period last year.

Soybeans stored in all positions on December 1, 2025 totaled 3.29 billion 
bushels, up 6 percent from December 1, 2024. Soybean stocks stored on farms 
totaled 1.58 billion bushels, up 2 percent from a year ago. Off-farm stocks, 
at 1.71 billion bushels, are up 10 percent from last December. Indicated 
disappearance for September - November 2025 totaled 1.30 billion bushels, 
down 20 percent from the same period a year earlier.

All wheat stored in all positions on December 1, 2025 totaled 1.68 billion 
bushels, up 7 percent from a year ago. On-farm stocks are estimated at 
446 million bushels, down 4 percent from last December. Off-farm stocks, at 
1.23 billion bushels, are up 11 percent from a year ago. The 
September - November 2025 indicated disappearance is 459 million bushels, 
9 percent above the same period a year earlier.
 
Durum wheat stored in all positions on December 1, 2025 totaled 61.1 million 
bushels, up 8 percent from a year ago. On-farm stocks, at 40.9 million 
bushels, are up 8 percent from December 1, 2024. Off-farm stocks totaled 
20.2 million bushels, up 8 percent from a year ago. The 
September - November 2025 indicated disappearance of 10.8 million bushels is 
slightly above the same period a year earlier.

Barley stored in all positions on December 1, 2025 totaled 121 million 
bushels, up 3 percent from December 1, 2024. On-farm stocks are estimated at 
68.9 million bushels, 4 percent above a year ago. Off-farm stocks, at 
51.8 million bushels, are 2 percent above December 2024. The 
September - November 2025 indicated disappearance is 29.4 million bushels, 
20 percent below the same period a year earlier.

Oats stored in all positions on December 1, 2025 totaled 56.0 million 
bushels, up 7 percent from the stocks on December 1, 2024. Of the total 
stocks on hand, 28.7 million bushels are stored on farms, up 13 percent from 
a year ago. Off-farm stocks totaled 27.3 million bushels, up 2 percent from 
the previous year. Indicated disappearance during September - November 2025 
totaled 8.03 million bushels.

Grain sorghum stored in all positions on December 1, 2025 totaled 268 million 
bushels, up 26 percent from a year ago. On-farm stocks, at 39.7 million 
bushels, are up 26 percent from December 1 last year. Off-farm stocks, at 
228 million bushels, are up 26 percent from a year earlier. The 
September - November 2025 indicated disappearance from all positions is 
209 million bushels, up 27 percent from the same period in 2024.

Pulse crops stored in all positions on December 1, 2025 are: dry edible peas, 
9.43 million cwt; lentils, 6.11 million cwt; all chickpeas, 4.38 million cwt; 
small chickpeas, 1.64 million cwt; and large chickpeas, 2.74 million cwt.

This report was approved on January 12, 2026.

Quick Stats

QuickStats API

Introduction

Terms of Service

Usage

Request API Key

The National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) offers Quick Stats, an on-line database containing official published aggregate estimates related to U.S. agricultural production. NASS develops these estimates from data collected through:

  1. 1) hundreds of sample surveys conducted each year covering virtually every aspect of U.S. agriculture
  2. 2) the Census of Agriculture conducted every five years providing state- and county-level aggregates

The Quick Stats application programming interface (API) provides direct access to the statistical information in the Quick Stats database. We invite developers to use this API and to give us feedback so we can continue to improve it.

About the Quick Stats API

To use the Quick Stats API, you must first agree to the NASS Terms of Service and obtain an API key In registering for the key, you must provide a valid email address. You will have the option to request future email updates about the Quick Stats API.

Once you request the API key, we will email it and you can proceed immediately. Use the key in all future data requests as well.
To call the Quick Stats API, you may use either of the following:

  • any language that supports HTTP GET request such as PHP, PERL, etc...
  • JSON with padding or JSONP

Your request will return a maximum of 50,000 data records. You can determine the returned record account before you execute the Quick Stats API call using the GET /api/get_counts function. If your request will return more than the maximum limit of 50,000 data records, you can do either of the following:

  • Change the filtering criteria (the API input parameters and their values) to generate a smaller number of responses
  • Download the files containing larger amounts of data extracted from the Quick Stats database.


Using QuickStats API
QuickStats API requests utilize input parameters based on the concept of What, Where and When.

  • What parameters refer to a commodity, data item or subject area.
  • Where parameters refer to a location or geographic level such as the entire United States, state, county, district, or ZIP code.
  • When parameters refer to a time such as year and frequency such as monthly.

Grain Stocks 

ISSN: 1949-0925

Released June 30, 2026, by the National Agricultural Statistics Service 
(NASS), Agricultural Statistics Board, United States Department of 
Agriculture (USDA).

Corn Stocks Up 14 Percent from June 2025
Soybean Stocks Up 5 Percent
All Wheat Stocks Up 8 Percent

Corn stocks in all positions on June 1, 2026 totaled 5.29 billion bushels, up 
14 percent from June 1, 2025. Of the total stocks, 2.96 billion bushels are 
stored on farms, up 16 percent from a year earlier. Off-farm stocks, at 
2.34 billion bushels, are up 12 percent from a year ago. The March - May 2026 
indicated disappearance is 3.74 billion bushels, compared with 3.50 billion 
bushels during the same period last year.

Soybeans stored in all positions on June 1, 2026 totaled 1.06 billion 
bushels, up 5 percent from June 1, 2025. On-farm stocks totaled 367 million 
bushels, down 11 percent from a year ago. Off-farm stocks, at 694 million 
bushels, are up 16 percent from a year ago. Indicated disappearance for the 
March - May 2026 quarter totaled 1.06 billion bushels, up 18 percent from the 
same period a year earlier.

Old crop all wheat stored in all positions on June 1, 2026 totaled 
920 million bushels, up 8 percent from a year ago. On-farm stocks are 
estimated at 177 million bushels, down 4 percent from last year. Off-farm 
stocks, at 743 million bushels, are up 11 percent from a year ago. The 
March - May 2026 indicated disappearance is 383 million bushels, up slightly 
from the same period a year earlier.

Old crop Durum wheat stocks in all positions on June 1, 2026 totaled 
33.5 million bushels, up 20 percent from a year ago. On-farm stocks, at 
18.6 million bushels, are up 32 percent from June 1, 2025. Off-farm stocks 
totaled 14.9 million bushels, up 8 percent from a year ago. The 
March - May 2026 indicated disappearance of 12.3 million bushels is up 
17 percent from the same period a year earlier.

Old crop barley stocks in all positions on June 1, 2026 totaled 66.4 million 
bushels, down 4 percent from June 1, 2025. On-farm stocks are estimated at 
23.5 million bushels, 12 percent above a year ago. Off-farm stocks, at 
42.9 million bushels, are 12 percent below June 1, 2025. The March - May 2026 
indicated disappearance is 26.7 million bushels, 20 percent below the same 
period a year earlier.

Old crop oats stored in all positions on June 1, 2026 totaled 31.8 million 
bushels, 12 percent above the stocks on June 1, 2025. Of the total stocks on 
hand, 13.9 million bushels are stored on farms, 42 percent above a year ago. 
Off-farm stocks totaled 17.9 million bushels, 4 percent below the previous 
year. Indicated disappearance during March - May 2026 totaled 9.17 million 
bushels, 34 percent below the same period a year ago.

Grain sorghum stored in all positions on June 1, 2026 totaled 66.7 million 
bushels, down 33 percent from a year ago. On-farm stocks, at 8.61 million 
bushels, are up 25 percent from last year. Off-farm stocks, at 58.1 million 
bushels, are down 37 percent from June 1, 2025. The March - May 2026 
indicated disappearance from all positions is 105 million bushels, up 
107 percent from the same period last year.

Pulse crops stored in all positions on June 1, 2026 and the change from 
June 1, 2025 are: dry edible peas, 3.92 million cwt, up 19 percent; lentils, 
3.08 million cwt, up 94 percent; all chickpeas, 2.48 million cwt, up 
40 percent; small chickpeas, 965 thousand cwt, up 68 percent; and large 
chickpeas, 1.52 million cwt, up 27 percent. Small chickpeas are defined as 
peas that will pass through a 20/64 inch round hole screen. Large chickpeas 
are defined as larger than 20/64 inches.

This report was approved on June 30, 2026.

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Grain Stocks
Description: Issued four times yearly, contains stocks of all wheat, durum wheat, corn, sorghum, oats, barley, soybeans, flaxseed, canola, rapeseed, rye, sunflower, safflower, mustard seed, by States and U.S. and by position (on-farm or off-farm storage); includes number and capacity of off-farm storage facilities and capacity of on-farm storage facilities. The data is obtained via an off and on-farm stocks survey, the on-farm survey is a probability survey of farm operators, the off-farm stocks survey is enumerates the volume of grain in all known commercial grain storage facilities.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Research report: USDA **Grain Stocks**

**Research checked: October 9, 2026.** This report distinguishes verified agency documentation from analytical interpretations and preservation recommendations.

## Executive findings

**Your description is substantially accurate—and reproduces the description in USDA’s publication catalog—but it is not a complete specification of the current data.** Important qualifications are:

- **Grain Stocks is a recurring statistical report and associated aggregate data series**, not a public file of individual farm or warehouse responses.
- USDA’s **National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS)** produces it through the **Agricultural Statistics Board (ASB)**.
- It is designated a **Principal Federal Economic Indicator**.
- The report appears four times a year, but **not every commodity or storage-capacity measure is published quarterly**.
- Current reporting includes **pulse crops—dry edible peas, lentils, and chickpeas—which your description omits**.
- On-farm estimates come from a probability survey. Off-farm collection attempts a **census of known eligible storage operations**, but missing responses require statistical adjustment. “Enumeration” does not mean every published value was directly observed.
- The principal collection authority is **7 U.S.C. § 2204(a)**. Participation in the two grain-stock surveys is **voluntary**; respondent confidentiality is protected by federal law.
- Historical continuity reaches back to **quarterly farm-stock estimates in 1926** and **all-position stock reports in 1943**.
- Preservation must retain **publication vintages, revisions, questionnaires, methodology, and quality measures**, not merely the latest database values.

The primary starting points are the [USDA publication archive](https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/publication/grain-stocks), [NASS survey guide](https://www.nass.usda.gov/Surveys/Guide_to_NASS_Surveys/Off-Farm_Grain_Stocks/), and [2026 methodology and quality report](https://data.nass.usda.gov/Publications/Methodology_and_Data_Quality/Grain_Stocks/02_2026/gsq0226.pdf).

---

## 1. Identity, publisher, and stewardship

| Attribute | Verified information |
|---|---|
| Official title | **Grain Stocks** |
| Producer | **National Agricultural Statistics Service**, U.S. Department of Agriculture |
| Official estimating/publication body | **Agricultural Statistics Board** |
| Resource type | Report, with associated published statistical estimates |
| Status | Active in USDA’s catalog |
| Frequency | Four regular releases annually; catalog metadata labels this “Seasonal” |
| ISSN | **1949-0925** |
| Current archive | USDA **Economics, Statistics, and Market Information System (ESMIS)**, hosted by the National Agricultural Library |
| ESMIS publication ID | **1480** |
| ESMIS identifier | **GraiStoc** |
| Main subject | Grains and oilseeds |
| Public observation level | Primarily United States and state aggregates, with some grouped or unallocated categories |
| Latest release listed when checked | **September 30, 2026**, reporting September 1, 2026 stocks |

The [publication metadata API](https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/api/v1/publication/findById/1480) independently confirms the title, active status, resource type, identifiers, and availability of subscriptions.

**Stewardship distinction:** NASS is the statistical producer. The National Agricultural Library provides the publication archive. Quick Stats is a separate NASS dissemination database. Neither the archive host nor a third-party data distributor should be mistaken for the original publisher.

---

## 2. What the data measures—and corrections to your description

### A. Core concept: inventories at a particular date

The dataset measures **physical quantities of specified agricultural commodities in storage on a reference date**, separated by storage position:

- **On-farm**
- **Off-farm**
- **Total, all positions**

Off-farm stocks include holdings at mills, elevators, warehouses, terminals, and processors.

This is a **stock**, not a flow. It is not the same as annual production, sales, exports, warehouse throughput, or forecast future supply.

“Position” describes storage location/category, **not necessarily ownership**. Grain owned by a farmer but stored at a commercial elevator is not automatically an on-farm stock.

### B. Commodity coverage and frequency

The [2026 methodology report](https://data.nass.usda.gov/Publications/Methodology_and_Data_Quality/Grain_Stocks/02_2026/gsq0226.pdf) distinguishes:

| Publication frequency | Commodities/measures |
|---|---|
| Quarterly | Corn, sorghum, oats, barley, all wheat, durum wheat, soybeans |
| Twice yearly | Sunflower stocks, referenced to March 1 and September 1 |
| Twice yearly | Dry edible peas, lentils, and chickpeas, referenced to June 1 and December 1 |
| Annual, in selected issues | Canola, mustard seed, rapeseed, rye, and safflower |
| Annual December 1 infrastructure statistics, published in January | On-farm storage capacity; off-farm facility number and storage capacity |

The catalog and survey guide also list **flaxseed**, including June reporting. This is different from a statute expressly requiring a publication titled *Grain Stocks* on four particular dates. The sources reviewed establish a continuing statistical program under general USDA authority and federal statistical oversight—not a stand-alone “Grain Stocks Act.”

See the [2021 Federal Register collection notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2021-07-30/pdf/2021-16257.pdf).

## 5. How the estimates are produced

The [2026 methodology report](https://data.nass.usda.gov/Publications/Methodology_and_Data_Quality/Grain_Stocks/02_2026/gsq0226.pdf) is the key technical source.

### A. On-farm: Quarterly Agricultural Survey

**Target population:** farms with cropland and/or storage capacity.

**Coverage:** all states except Hawaii, according to current methodology.

**Design:**

- A **list frame** of known agricultural operations.
- An **area frame** to cover farms not adequately represented on the list.
- Multivariate probability-proportional-to-size sampling for the list component.
- Replication and a designated stocks panel to help measure quarter-to-quarter change.

The area-frame contribution includes operations **not on the list**, commonly described as the NOL component.

**Estimation:**

- Direct expansion using survey weights.
- Ratio estimators, including relationships between current and previous stocks and between stocks, production, and capacity.
- Imputation for missing responses.
- Manual imputation for certain large or atypical operations.

Thus, the estimates are not simple sums of respondents’ reported inventories.

### B. Off-farm: Grain Stocks Report/OFGS survey

**Target population:** known off-farm entities capable of storing **at least 1,000 bushels**, including elevators, processing plants, terminals, and other qualifying storage operations.

**Coverage:** conducted in all states except Alaska, Connecticut, Hawaii, Nevada, and Rhode Island, according to the 2026 methodology.

**Design:** a census of known eligible operations, stratified by capacity and specialty/non-specialty characteristics for nonresponse adjustment.

**Nonresponse treatment:**

- Capacity-based adjustment in lower strata.
- Manual imputation for larger operations in higher strata.

This supports a more precise version of your description:

> The off-farm survey attempts to enumerate known eligible commercial storage operations; published estimates also account for nonresponding operations.

A census of a known frame remains vulnerable to missing facilities, inaccurate frame information, reporting errors, and nonresponse.

### C. Review and reconciliation

Regional Field Offices edit and analyze responses, generate survey summaries, and recommend estimates. Headquarters and the ASB review and reconcile state and national estimates.

NASS also uses a **national balance-sheet check**, comparing stocks with external information such as:

- Imports.
- Exports.
- Food processing and soybean crushing.
- Feed and seed use.
- Industrial use, including ethanol production.

**Official estimates are therefore reviewed statistical estimates, not an untouched output of one survey estimator.**

## 6. Timing, publication lag, and revisions

### Reference dates versus release dates

| Inventory reference date | Normal publication timing |
|---|---|
| March 1 | Late March |
| June 1 | Late June |
| September 1 | Late September |
| December 1 | Early January of the following year |

Collection lasts approximately 15 calendar days, followed by regional and national editing and review.

A critical example: **the January 12, 2026 report describes December 1, 2025 stocks**, not January 2026 inventories.

### Revision policy

NASS documents revisions:

- In the quarter following initial publication.
- Again in the December 1 report published in January.
- During five-year reviews following the Census of Agriculture.

Consequently, the same reference-date observation can appear with different values in successive releases.

For example, national December 1, 2025 corn stocks were **13,282,366 thousand bushels** in the January 2026 issue, but **13,305,825 thousand bushels** in the June 2026 issue. These are different publication vintages of the same inventory date, not two separate observations.

Sources: [January issue](https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/sites/default/release-files/795726/grst0126.txt) and [June issue](https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/sites/default/release-files/795959/grst0626.txt).

**For forecasting, event studies, or market backtesting, preserve what was publicly known at the time.** Using later revisions can introduce look-ahead bias.

## 7. Quality, uncertainty, and limitations

### Published quality documentation

NASS publishes an annual **Grain Stocks Methodology and Quality Measures** report with:

- Survey sample sizes.
- Response rates.
- Weighted item response rates.
- Coefficients of variation (CVs).
- Sampling, imputation, estimation, and revision explanations.

The 2026 report covers the preceding eight quarters in several quality tables.

A CV is the standard error divided by the estimate, expressed as a percentage. NASS reports that over the preceding decade, national Agricultural Survey CVs ranged approximately:

- **Corn:** 1.5%–4.4%.
- **Soybeans:** 1.7%–7.5%.
- **All wheat:** 2.3%–5.0%.

These are **survey-estimator precision measures**, not a universal error bound for every official published stock estimate.

### Why the census is not error-free

The off-farm survey has no sampling error in the ordinary census-design sense. However, its published quality tables still include CV measures associated with estimation and nonresponse uncertainty.

NASS explicitly cautions that calculated CVs do not fully capture:

- Reporting errors.
- Manual imputation errors.
- Differences in storage behavior between respondents and nonrespondents.

### Nonresponse deserves attention

The April 2026 OMB approval expressly authorized larger Quarterly Agricultural Survey samples **to counter declining response rates**.

That is an important policy and methodological development. A larger sample may improve precision, but it does not automatically eliminate nonresponse bias.

### What the public data cannot establish

By themselves, these aggregates do not provide:

- Warehouse-level inventories or addresses.
- Firm ownership or market shares.
- Grain condition, contamination, or spoilage.
- A complete shipment or logistics network.
- Household food access or hunger.
- Local environmental or occupational harms.
- A causal explanation for price movements.

They can support such research when linked to additional evidence, but should not be represented as measuring those outcomes directly.

## 10. Data-science handling rules

### Essential parsing and modeling cautions

1. **Separate three dates:** inventory reference date, publication release date, and retrieval/load date.
2. **Retain units and multipliers:** a table value in “1,000 bushels” is not already a bushel count.
3. **Do not double-count hierarchies:** durum/all wheat; small and large/all chickpeas; storage components/total.
4. **Distinguish missingness:** `(D)` means withheld for disclosure protection; `(NA)` means unavailable. Neither means zero.
5. **Retain blank-cell explanations:** recent national tables say some blanks indicate an estimation period not yet begun.
6. **Preserve unallocated categories:** national totals need not equal the sum of visible named states.
7. **Check footnotes before enforcing identities:** disclosure treatment and rounding can complicate apparent additivity.
8. **Model seasonality and marketing years:** adjacent-quarter changes often reflect harvest timing.
9. **Interpret indicated disappearance carefully:** it is a supply-accounting measure, not a directly surveyed breakdown of feed, exports, ethanol, and other uses.
10. **Use vintage-aware data for historical decisions:** later revisions were unavailable to contemporaneous users.

A useful normalized record would contain:

```text
commodity / class
measure
storage_position
geography / geography_code
reference_date
value / unit / multiplier
status_flag
release_date / vintage
source_file / table / footnotes
retrieval_timestamp
```

This is a **recommended analytical schema**, not USDA’s native schema.

- **Additional program-use evidence:** A [Federal Register notice from 1999](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-1999-07-08/html/99-17255.htm) connects the collection to farm-program legislation and export-import decisions.
- **No Known Issue argument:** Its established federal use, explicit legal authority, and economic-indicator status provide institutional protection. However, the reviewed sources do not establish a statutory obligation to maintain this particular publication unchanged.
- **Substitutes:** I did not identify a public alternative offering equivalent national/state, on-/off-farm coverage. Other USDA supply-and-demand products are not independent replacements simply because they report related quantities.

### Selected level: **High Risk**

**Under your rubric’s disjunctive wording, broad rather than dataset-specific authorization is enough to trigger High Risk.** This does **not** mean that authority is legally doubtful or that programmatic use is absent.

A Moderate Risk rating would also be defensible if “required for implementation” includes longstanding operational dependence. I selected High Risk because the sources document use, but do not establish a binding requirement to preserve the specific collection.

**Confidence: Moderate; the rubric’s legal categories overlap.**

## 5. Staffing and Funding

### Evidence by risk level

- **High Risk:** The American Statistical Association’s [2025 NASS assessment](https://www.amstat.org/docs/default-source/amstat-documents/the-nations-data-at-risk-2025/national-agricultural-statistics-service.pdf) estimates **41% staffing loss since FY2024**. An [AEI report dated January 15, 2026](https://www.aei.org/research-products/report/the-looming-data-imperative-to-inform-agricultural-policy/) reports **40% lost during FY2025**. Both meet your 40% threshold.
- **Primary-source corroboration, with measurement caveats:** USDA’s [FY2026 explanatory notes](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/documents/19-2026-CJ-NASS.pdf) describe a reduction from **754 to 495 staff**, approximately **34%**. Its [FY2027 notes](https://usda.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/documents/FY-2027-Chapter-19-NASS.pdf) describe **754 to 489**, approximately **35%**. Those comparisons alone fall in Moderate Risk.
- The FY2027 notes also show discretionary-funded FTEs declining from **707 in FY2024 to an estimated 389 in FY2026**, approximately **45%**. **FTEs are not employee headcounts**, and estimated budget staffing should not be presented as a verified count of completed separations.
- **Funding counterevidence:** The FY2026 notes show $187.85 million for FY2025 versus a $185 million FY2026 request—about **1.5% lower**, not a 20% cut. The FY2027 request is $187.455 million. Requests and estimates are not interchangeable with final enacted appropriations or actual spending.
- **Tracker limitation:** The requested [USAJobs tracker](https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com) states that collection stopped on **December 31, 2025** and warns that job listings are **not actual hires**. It cannot independently establish current NASS staffing losses.
- **Gone:** Neither staffing nor funding has been eliminated.

### Selected level: **High Risk**

The reported 40–41% staffing losses meet the threshold, supported by strong primary-source evidence of substantial workforce contraction. **The rating is staffing-driven, not based on a demonstrated 20% budget cut.**

**Confidence: Moderate**, because sources use different periods, staffing definitions, and actual-versus-estimated figures. Grain Stocks-specific staff losses were not identified.
